points.title: Comparing and ordering integers
points.brief: Integers are whole numbers and their negatives. On a number line, numbers to the right are larger, so -2 is greater than -7.

points.title: Adding and subtracting integers
points.brief: Adding a negative is the same as subtracting, and subtracting a negative is the same as adding, so 5 - (-3) = 8. Using a number line to check.

points.title: Multiplying and dividing integers
points.brief: Two numbers with the same sign give a positive product or quotient, and different signs give a negative one, so -6 × -4 = 24 and 18 ÷ -3 = -6.

points.title: Order of operations with integers
points.brief: Brackets first, then powers, then multiplying and dividing from left to right, then adding and subtracting from left to right, keeping track of negative signs at each step.

points.title: Equivalent fractions and comparing fractions
points.brief: Multiplying or dividing the top and bottom by the same number gives an equivalent fraction. To compare fractions, rewrite them with a common denominator.

points.title: Adding and subtracting fractions
points.brief: Rewrite the fractions with the lowest common denominator, then add or subtract the numerators. Mixed numbers can be changed to improper fractions first.

points.title: Multiplying and dividing fractions
points.brief: Multiply numerators together and denominators together. To divide, multiply by the reciprocal of the second fraction. Simplify the answer.

points.title: Rounding decimals
points.brief: Rounding a decimal to a given number of decimal places by looking at the next digit, 5 or more rounds up, and why a rounded answer is an approximation.

points.title: Recurring decimals and irrational numbers
points.brief: Some fractions give terminating decimals and others recurring ones, written with a dot or bar. A number such as pi or the square root of 2 is irrational, because its decimal never ends or repeats.

points.title: Converting fractions, decimals and percentages
points.brief: A percentage is a fraction out of 100. Moving between the three forms, such as 3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5%.

points.title: One quantity as a percentage of another
points.brief: Write the part over the whole as a fraction, with both in the same units, then multiply by 100 to get the percentage.

points.title: Finding a percentage of an amount
points.brief: Change the percentage to a decimal or fraction and multiply, so 15% of $80 is 0.15 × 80 = $12.

points.title: Percentage increase and decrease
points.brief: Increasing by 20% is multiplying by 1.2, and decreasing by 20% is multiplying by 0.8. Used for discounts, mark-ups and GST at 10%.

points.title: Simplifying ratios
points.brief: A ratio compares quantities of the same kind in the same units. Divide each part by the highest common factor, so 12 to 18 simplifies to 2 to 3.

points.title: Dividing a quantity in a ratio
points.brief: Add the parts of the ratio to find the total number of parts, find the value of one part, then multiply. $60 shared in the ratio 2 to 3 gives $24 and $36.

points.title: Rates and unit rates
points.brief: A rate compares quantities with different units, such as km per hour. A unit rate gives the amount for one unit and is used to find the best buy.

points.title: Distance-time graphs
points.brief: On a distance-time graph, a steeper line means a faster speed and a flat line means no movement. Reading speed from the graph as distance divided by time.

points.title: Pronumerals and writing expressions
points.brief: A pronumeral is a letter that stands for a number. Turning words into expressions, so 5 more than twice a number is 2n + 5.

points.title: Substitution
points.brief: Replacing each pronumeral with its value and working out the expression using the order of operations, such as 3a² when a = -2.

points.title: Adding and subtracting like terms
points.brief: Like terms have exactly the same pronumerals with the same powers. Only like terms can be added or subtracted, so 3x + 2y + 5x = 8x + 2y.

points.title: Multiplying and dividing algebraic terms
points.brief: Multiply the numbers, then the pronumerals, so 3a × 4b = 12ab. Dividing terms is simplifying a fraction, so 12xy ÷ 4x = 3y.

points.title: Expanding brackets
points.brief: The distributive law multiplies the term outside the brackets by every term inside, so 3(x - 4) = 3x - 12, watching the sign when a negative is outside.

points.title: Factorising with a common factor
points.brief: Factorising is expanding in reverse. Take out the highest common factor of every term, numbers and pronumerals, so 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3).

points.title: Prime factors in index form
points.brief: Writing a whole number as a product of primes with a factor tree, then in index form, so 72 = 2³ × 3².

points.title: Square roots and cube roots
points.brief: A square root undoes squaring and a cube root undoes cubing. Finding exact roots of perfect squares and cubes, and estimating others between two whole numbers.

points.title: Index laws for multiplying and dividing
points.brief: When multiplying powers of the same base, add the indices. When dividing, subtract them. So 2⁵ × 2³ = 2⁸ and 5⁶ ÷ 5² = 5⁴.

points.title: Power of a power and the zero index
points.brief: A power raised to a power multiplies the indices, so (3²)⁴ = 3⁸. Any non-zero number to the power 0 equals 1.

points.title: One-step equations
points.brief: An equation stays balanced when the same operation is done to both sides. Solving x + 7 = 12 or 4x = 20 with one inverse operation.

points.title: Two-step equations
points.brief: Undo the operations in reverse order, adding or subtracting first, then multiplying or dividing, so 3x - 5 = 16 gives x = 7.

points.title: Checking a solution by substitution
points.brief: Put the solution back into the original equation. If both sides come out equal, the solution is right.

points.title: Simple quadratic equations
points.brief: An equation such as x² = 49 has two solutions, x = 7 and x = -7, because squaring a negative also gives a positive.

points.title: The Cartesian plane
points.brief: Points are plotted as (x, y), across then up or down, on a plane with four quadrants. Naming the quadrant from the signs of the coordinates.

points.title: Tables of values
points.brief: Making a table of x and y values from a rule such as y = 2x + 1, then plotting the points. A linear relationship gives points in a straight line.

points.title: Solving equations with graphs
points.brief: Where two lines cross, both rules are true at once. Reading the x value where a line meets a height y solves the equation.

points.title: Perimeter of shapes and composite figures
points.brief: Perimeter is the distance around a shape. For a composite figure, work out any missing side lengths first, then add every outside edge.

points.title: Parts of a circle
points.brief: The centre, radius, diameter, chord, arc, sector, segment, tangent and circumference, and the fact that the diameter is twice the radius.

points.title: Circumference of a circle
points.brief: Pi is the circumference divided by the diameter, about 3.14. Circumference is pi times the diameter, or 2 times pi times the radius.

points.title: The hypotenuse and Pythagoras' theorem
points.brief: In a right-angled triangle, the hypotenuse is the longest side, opposite the right angle. The square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.

points.title: Finding the hypotenuse
points.brief: Square the two shorter sides, add them, then take the square root, so sides 6 and 8 give a hypotenuse of 10.

points.title: Finding a shorter side
points.brief: Square the hypotenuse, subtract the square of the known shorter side, then take the square root.

points.title: Testing for a right angle
points.brief: If the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two, the triangle is right-angled. Pythagorean triads such as 3, 4, 5 and 5, 12, 13.

points.title: Pythagoras' theorem in problems
points.brief: Drawing a diagram for a worded problem, such as a ladder against a wall or the diagonal of a rectangle, finding the right-angled triangle and solving it.

points.title: Area of rectangles, triangles and parallelograms
points.brief: A rectangle is length times width, a parallelogram is base times perpendicular height, and a triangle is half of base times perpendicular height.

points.title: Area of trapeziums, rhombuses and kites
points.brief: A trapezium is half the sum of the parallel sides times the height. A rhombus or kite is half the product of its diagonals.

points.title: Area of a circle
points.brief: The area of a circle is pi times the radius squared. Using the radius, not the diameter, is the common mistake to avoid.

points.title: Area of sectors and composite shapes
points.brief: A sector's area is the fraction of the circle given by its angle over 360. A composite shape is split into simple shapes, then areas are added or subtracted.

points.title: Converting units of area
points.brief: Since 1 cm = 10 mm, 1 cm² = 100 mm². In the same way 1 m² = 10,000 cm², and a hectare is 10,000 m². Choosing a sensible unit for an area.

points.title: Views of solids
points.brief: The front, side and top views of a prism or a solid built from prisms, and matching a solid to its views.

points.title: Volume of a prism
points.brief: The volume of any prism is the area of its cross-section times its length or height, V = Ah, with the answer in cubic units.

points.title: Volume of a cylinder
points.brief: A cylinder's cross-section is a circle, so its volume is pi times the radius squared times the height.

points.title: Volume and capacity units
points.brief: Converting between cubic units, and between volume and capacity, using 1 cm³ = 1 mL and 1 m³ = 1000 L.

points.title: Naming angles and geometry notation
points.brief: Naming an angle with three letters, the vertex in the middle, and the marks for equal sides, equal angles and parallel lines. Acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex and revolution.

points.title: Angles at a point and on a line
points.brief: Angles on a straight line add to 180°, angles at a point add to 360°, and vertically opposite angles are equal.

points.title: Angles and parallel lines
points.brief: When a transversal crosses parallel lines, corresponding angles are equal, alternate angles are equal and co-interior angles add to 180°.

points.title: Giving reasons for angles
points.brief: Finding unknown angles in steps and naming the rule used for each step, and using the angle rules to show that two lines are parallel.

points.title: Classifying triangles
points.brief: By sides, triangles are equilateral, isosceles or scalene. By angles, they are acute-angled, right-angled or obtuse-angled.

points.title: Angle sum and exterior angle of a triangle
points.brief: The angles of a triangle add to 180°. An exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles.

points.title: Classifying quadrilaterals
points.brief: Squares, rectangles, rhombuses, parallelograms, trapeziums and kites, and how one family includes another, such as a square being a special rectangle.

points.title: Properties of quadrilaterals
points.brief: Comparing quadrilaterals by their sides, angles and diagonals, such as whether the diagonals bisect each other or meet at right angles. The angles of any quadrilateral add to 360°.

points.title: Categorical and numerical data
points.brief: Categorical data sorts into groups, nominal with no order and ordinal with an order. Numerical data is counted (discrete) or measured (continuous).

points.title: Choosing a graph
points.brief: Which display suits which data, such as a column graph for categories, a line graph for change over time and a histogram for grouped numerical data.

points.title: Dot plots and stem-and-leaf plots
points.brief: Reading and building dot plots and stem-and-leaf plots, which keep every value and show where data clusters.

points.title: Reading graphs critically
points.brief: Interpreting what a graph shows, and spotting ways a graph can mislead, such as an axis that does not start at zero or uneven scales.

points.title: The mean
points.brief: The mean is the total of the values divided by how many values there are. Finding a missing value when the mean is known.

points.title: Median, mode and range
points.brief: The median is the middle value once the data is in order, the mode is the most common value, and the range is the highest minus the lowest.

points.title: The effect of an outlier
points.brief: An outlier is a value far from the rest. It pulls the mean towards it and changes the range a lot, but barely moves the median.

points.title: Comparing two datasets
points.brief: Comparing two groups by their centre and spread, and drawing a conclusion that the data supports.

points.title: Sample spaces and outcomes
points.brief: The sample space is the list of all possible outcomes. Outcomes are equally likely when each has the same chance, such as the faces of a fair die.

points.title: Theoretical probability
points.brief: The probability of an event is the number of favourable outcomes over the total number of equally likely outcomes, from 0 for impossible to 1 for certain.

points.title: Complementary events
points.brief: The complement of an event is the event not happening. The two probabilities add to 1, so P(not A) = 1 - P(A).

points.title: Experimental probability
points.brief: Relative frequency is the number of times an event happened over the number of trials. The more trials, the closer it tends to get to the theoretical probability.
